editorial.headline: Water-Resource Infrastructure Construction: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the construction and upkeep of water-resource infrastructure, open at every stated scale, with full foreign ownership nationally and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
Water-resource infrastructure construction is the category for creating, maintaining, or rebuilding the physical systems that capture, direct, store, regulate, or defend against water. Its remit reaches dams and weirs, small reservoirs, water gates and regulators, water-carrying viaducts and siphons, check dams, dikes and flood-control channels, free-intake works, reservoirs, and pumping stations. This is therefore a category defined by built water works rather than by one asset type: it covers both initial construction and the continuing work of maintenance or reconstruction on that infrastructure.

The activity is open across the scales stated in the record: Besar, Mikro, Kecil, and Menengah. That breadth matters because the category follows the nature of the construction work, not one company size. Its definition places the operational focus squarely on construction, maintenance, and/or rebuilding of the named water-resource infrastructure. It is a precise physical remit, spanning flow-control structures, water-storage works, intake structures, flood-control works, and pumping stations.

At national level, the record marks this activity TERBUKA and allows foreign ownership up to 100%. In plain terms, foreign participation is open nationally with full foreign ownership permitted under the stated national source. Bali’s result is not a concealed reversal of that national position. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record says that, at Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi; it is therefore not blocked by the provincial moratorium. That moratorium blocks PMA registrations for Low and Medium-Low risk activities island-wide and permanently. This activity does not fall into that blocked category on the Bali reading provided.

The distinction should remain crisp. National openness supplies the 100% foreign-ownership ceiling; Bali’s result says the province-wide PMA moratorium does not prohibit this activity. No Bali-specific ownership percentage or partnership condition is stated in the record. The responsible reading is straightforward: this is the category for actual water-resource infrastructure construction, maintenance, or rebuilding, and Bali’s moratorium is not the obstacle here.
